THE IDEA BEHIND DIRECT DETECTION
You know dark matter from gravity — this tries to touch it

Wait for a dark-matter particle
to bump a nucleus.

Halo dark matterstreams through the Earth
→
Rare collisionone particle hits a xenon nucleus
→
A tiny recoilthe nucleus gets a keV-scale kick

That faint recoil — a nucleus knocked by a few tens to hundreds of keV — is the whole signal. Billions of dark-matter particles cross the detector, and you hope to catch the handful that actually touch something.

WHY THIS PAPER LOOKS HIGHER
Not all dark matter kicks the same way

Most searches expect
gentle kicks. Some models
kick harder.

The textbook particle (a “WIMP”) gives mostly low-energy recoils — so experiments zoom in there and ignore the rest.

But two ideas push the kick higher: a broader menu of possible interactions where the force grows with collision momentum; and “inelastic” dark matter that must turn into a slightly heavier cousin when it hits — which costs energy.

Both hide in the high-energy range standard analyses discard. So LZ looked there — up to 270 keV.

Fig. 1 · expected recoil spectra. Bottom: a heavy WIMP (brown, 1000 GeV) peaks near 200 keV, where a light one (red, 50 GeV) has died off. Top: inelastic models (δ>0) suppress low energy. Grey = low detector efficiency.
DEEPER · READING FIGURE 1
Every curve is a different WIMP–nucleus interaction

What O₁ˢ and L₁₀ˢ mean.

One framework — non-relativistic effective field theory — writes the WIMP–nucleon coupling as a sum of every allowed operator, built from the momentum transfer q, the relative velocity v, and the WIMP & nucleon spins (15 in all). Each label on the plot is one such operator.

The labels

O₁ˢ — the standard spin-independent coupling (to nucleon number): the “vanilla” WIMP. (top panel)

L₁₀ˢ — a magnetic-moment interaction (a relativistic form reduced to NR); picked for its broad, double-peaked spectrum. (bottom panel)

superscript s / v — isoscalar (protons & neutrons alike) vs isovector (opposite signs).

Reading the two panels

Top — inelastic, varying δ. δ is the mass splitting: the WIMP up-scatters to a state heavier by δ. δ=0 is elastic; a larger δ needs a minimum energy, killing low-energy recoils and shifting weight up (0 / 200 / 300 keV).

Bottom — elastic, three masses. Heavier WIMPs (1000 GeV) push the peak to high energy.

The wiggles. Dips are xenon form-factor (nuclear-response) minima; the operators' momentum (q²) dependence lifts the high-energy bump — exactly why these models need the extended window.

HOW YOU KNOW IT WAS A NUCLEUS
7 tonnes of liquid xenon

Every kick makes
two flashes:
light and charge.

A collision makes a prompt flash of light and a cloud of charge that drifts up — two signals per event. Their ratio tells a recoiling nucleus (what dark matter would do) from a knocked-loose electron (the common radioactive background). That separation is what makes the search possible.

tonne·year of data
220
days (2023–24)
≤270
keV recoils probed

The bands come from calibration with sources of known recoil type: injected beta-emitters (tritium and ¹⁴C) trace the electron band; neutron sources (a D–D generator and AmBe) knock xenon nuclei to trace the nuclear band.

Fig. 2 · calibration data. Electron-recoil sources (blue/green) trace the upper band; nuclear-recoil sources (orange/purple) the lower one — the light-to-charge ratio cleanly separates them.
WHAT THEY FOUND
Reading the plot's two axes

A kick at 248 keV —
and it looks like
a nucleus.

The axes are the detector's two signals. S1 is the prompt flash of scintillation light at the instant of the recoil — it scales with the deposited energy. S2 is the charge: electrons freed by the recoil drift up, get pulled into a thin gas layer, and make a second, amplified flash whose size measures the ionization. (“c” = position-corrected; “phd” = photons detected.)

S1c
prompt light — scales with energy
S2c
drifted charge — the ionization

Their ratio is the discriminator: a nucleus makes less charge per unit light than an electron, so nuclear recoils (red band) sit below electron recoils (blue). The event, at S1c ≈ 540 phd, lands on the red band — nucleus-like, at 2.6σ.

Fig. 4 · light (S1) vs charge (S2). The candidate is the isolated point at right, on the nuclear-recoil band (red) — far from the electron background (blue/grey).
DEEPER · WHY THE SIGNAL IS SO CLEAN
Yes, there are nuclear-recoil backgrounds — they're just crushed

Why the signal region is so clean.

01
Self-shielding + a fiducial cut

Dense, high-Z xenon soaks up radiation from the edges; only the clean inner core is analysed, so external neutrons rarely reach it.

02
Single-scatter only

A WIMP scatters once. Neutrons usually scatter several times — multiple charge (S2) pulses — and are thrown out.

03
Active vetoes around the detector

An outer gadolinium-loaded scintillator and a xenon “skin” tag neutrons (via capture γ-rays) and reject them.

04
High energy is intrinsically quiet

Almost every background — β's, γ's, even solar / atmospheric-neutrino recoils — piles up at low energy and falls off. The hundreds-of-keV window is nearly empty.

What survives — a few radiogenic / fission neutrons and irreducible atmospheric-neutrino (CEνNS) recoils — totals a fraction of an event. That's why a single event is only 2.6σ.

THE MAIN RESULT
Mostly nothing — and that is the result

The tightest limits yet
on these dark-matter
models.

Because the data look like background almost everywhere, the payoff is exclusion: LZ rules out a large swathe of these higher-energy dark-matter interactions — the strongest constraints to date, beating earlier experiments.

Astronomer’s translation: another big chunk of dark-matter parameter space is now closed off.

Fig. 6 · exclusion limits (this work: black, dashed = expected, green/yellow = sensitivity bands). Top: inelastic model vs mass splitting — below LUX 2021 (red) & LZ 2024a (purple). Bottom: elastic model vs WIMP mass — below PandaX-II 2019 (blue) & LZ 2024b (purple). Lower = stronger.
TAKEAWAYS
Three things to remember

In one minute.

→
A new place to look

Direct-detection experiments watch for dark matter kicking a nucleus. Pushing that search to higher recoil energies opens models that standard analyses miss.

→
One curious event

A single 248 keV nucleus-like kick at 2.6σ — short of the 5σ discovery bar. Watch this space, but it is not a detection.

→
The tightest limits yet

With essentially no signal, LZ sets the strongest constraints so far on these exotic dark-matter interactions — same detector, just a wider energy window.
